docs.dcterms_abstract:
A very long argument by one not personally acquainted
with D, provoked by perusal of D's treatise "The Case
in view". He argues about the exclusive authority of
the rightful possessor of a bishop's see to present
communion to all subjects in his diocese and the
schismatic behaviour of partaking at the hands of the
foreign bishop (i. e. one from a strange diocese) or a
deprived bishop. The people in the several districts
(Norwich only excepted) must be united to the present
actual Possessors as their Bishop and Head, and it is
as necessary to live in communion with him as it is for
them to be united to their true pastor in order to
communion with the Catholic Church and with Christ as
its head. He is exercised about the canonical status
of the deprived clergy. He argues about the danger of
Contagion put forward in D's treatise viz. of being 

 gained over by the opinions of the infected party.
Hence the possible disapproval of a rival Bp. by the
present diocesan. But he sees in Christ's not
refusing communion with the Jewish Church a precedent
for quiet submission even to disputable titles and
he wishes for the spirit of reconciliation and happy
reunion which he attributes to D, He would like D.
to answer, if he thinks the writer who is not
acquainted with him worthy of one.

Miss Anderson and Mrs Atkins, their next-door-neighbours, had moved very suddenly without telling anyone. Their sisters Polly and Betsy were in London yesterday dining with Mr Rawstorn and drinking tea with Uncle Gregory—Uncle Gregory and Aunt Sally and family are all very well. She encloses a short poem about a young shepherdess who is carefree. She closes the letter by saying it is late, and she must go to bed soon, and that her sister Polly is not very well. docs.dcterms_abstract:
Thinks B. has made an unhappy choice for the subject of
his book, for learned women are ridiculed at the
present time. Has found Lady Pakington's Prayers
and will send B. a transcript. Wants to know what was
the MS. he saw at Queens College, and how it came there. [Bodleian card catalogue]


Apologises for not writing sooner, pleading poor health. Sympathises with his
disappointments and expresses cynicism as to the current lack of concern with
learning. Fears that education, especially in women, is undervalued. Inquires
whether he would care for Lady Packington’s prayers, which she has finally
found. [Dawn Hollis]
